notes.1a: (i) The variation in atomic radius from silicon to sulfur was, in general, well known.
notes.1aii: Many candidates appreciated that the differences in melting points were a consequence of the differences in structures. Identification of the types and relative strengths of the forces of attraction broken during melting were referred to less often. Common misconceptions included the presence of intermolecular forces in silicon or did not refer to intermolecular forces, neither in general terms, nor as instantaneous dipole induced dipole attractions in sulfur.
notes.1b: (i) Most candidates correctly calculated the number of electrons in p subshells.
notes.1bii: Many equations showed appropriate species. State symbols, essential in any equation to represent the first ionisation energy process, were included less often.
notes.1iii: Candidates with an excellent knowledge of the trend in ionisation energy across a period identified the correct ionisation energy for phosphorus. They explained both the general trend and the effect of spin pair repulsion on a pair of electrons in a p orbital of sulfur compared to phosphorus. Weaker candidates either identified the value which represents a general trend in ionisation energy across the period and explained this trend or identified the correct value for ionisation energy with details that only explained why sulfur had a lower first ionisation energy than phosphorus.
notes.1iv: This was answered well by most candidates.
notes.1v: Appropriate description of the shape of an SCl molecule as ‘bent’ or ‘v-shape’ was seen often. ‘Linear’ was a common incorrect answer.
notes.2a: Some candidates appeared to confuse graphs of rate versus time with those showing concentration versus time.
notes.2b: Well-rehearsed arguments related the significance of increasing temperature on the position of equilibrium to the example given. More able candidates showed no ambiguity and made explicit reference to the effect of an increase in temperature on the position of this equilibrium in terms of either the ‘forward reaction is exothermic’ or ‘the reverse reaction is endothermic’. Less precise answers included ‘the reaction moves backwards as it’s an exothermic reaction’.
notes.2c: This question proved to be demanding. A few candidates found K using an appropriate method; they worked out the mole fraction of the components, converted them into partial pressures and then substituted these values into the correct expression for K . Weaker candidates calculated K p p directly from moles and included moles in the units. Deduction of units also presented difficulties. Many answers gave units in terms of Pa with no attempt to convert kPa to Pa within the calculation.
notes.2d: Lightning was well known as a natural process responsible for formation of atmospheric NO and NO . ‘Catalytic converter’ as the man-made process was a common incorrect answer.
notes.2e: (i) Many correct definitions of the term free radical were seen. Ambiguous descriptions referred to ‘unpaired electron’ as ‘unshared’ or ‘unbonded’ or ‘free’. Common incorrect answers referred to a free radical as ‘a species with a lone pair of electrons’.
notes.2eii: The pair of equations which showed the catalytic role of NO in the oxidation of SO were not well 2 2 known. The equation to represent the regeneration of NO appeared to cause most difficulties with many incorrectly balanced equations seen.
notes.2iii: Identification of the change in thermal stability down Group 2 nitrates was fairly well known.
notes.2f: (i) Identification of a magnesium containing base was relatively common. Incorrect answers included salts, rather than bases, which contained magnesium or bases that were not made from magnesium. The formula of the compound identified was not always correct.
notes.2fii: This equation proved challenging for many. Some answers incorrectly balanced equations which included all correct species. Use of an incorrect formula for magnesium nitrate was a common error, including Mg N . 3 2
notes.3a: (i) Fully balanced equations were seen by more able candidates.
notes.3aii: This definition was described accurately in most candidates answers. A common misconception was seen in weaker responses that described a weak acid as one that ‘did not completely dissolve’.
notes.3b: (i) Many candidates gave a definition of the enthalpy change which occurs when ‘one mole of product is formed from its elements’. It was less common for the elements to be described as ‘in their standard states’.
notes.3bii: More able candidates gave excellent and logical workings that contained clearly labelled energy cycles. It was common to see an expression for the different bond energies added or subtracted from each other, in a variety of possible incorrect combinations, with no attempt to show how these expressions were deduced. The stoichiometry of the equation was ignored by some.
notes.3iii: Description of this esterification reaction as a condensation reaction was relatively well known. Incorrect answers included hydrolysis and oxidation.
notes.3c: (i) Some candidates identified A as steam or H O(g), other candidates were less precise and identified A as water. A common incorrect answer was NaOH.
notes.3cii: Many unambiguous representations of 2-bromopropane were seen. Occasionally the central carbon atom was drawn with a valency of 3.
notes.3iv: This question proved to be demanding. Candidates were expected to ignore all bonds which were common to both reactant and product. While the appropriate bond, C=O, was identified in many answers C-O and C-H were also seen. Most candidates only identified a range of wavenumbers where a change in absorption occurs rather than described if the absorption appeared, disappeared or moved.
notes.3d: (i) More able candidates deduced a formula for the correct organic product in the equation. The inclusion of H O as the additional product was less common, even when included the equation was not always balanced.
notes.3dii: The appropriate formula to deduce the number of carbon atoms present in T was not well known and many confused calculations were seen. It was common for candidates to give a structural formula for T rather than the required molecular formula.
notes.4a: (i) Some candidates gave clear explanations of the presence of a chiral carbon in the lactic acid structure. A few candidates stated that optical isomers had chiral centres or described the behaviour of an optical isomer in the presence of polarised light.
notes.4aii: Many candidates were unable to give the systematic name of lactic acid. ‘Carboxylic acid’ was seen frequently.
notes.4iii: This question was demanding. Many candidates confused the reagents and conditions required to convert halogenoalkanes to nitriles with those required to convert ethanal to a hydroxynitrile. Deduction of the reagents and conditions used in the second step of both synthesis from propene and ethanal proved demanding for most candidates. Oxidising agents were more commonly seen for the third steps, however, some candidates represented the oxidising agents with incorrect formulae or with no reference to acid conditions.
notes.4b: (i) Some clear and precise reaction mechanisms were shown with partial charges assigned to relevant atoms and unambiguous representation of curly arrows to show bonds broken and bonds made. When drawing mechanisms of this type candidates should be encouraged to consider what the curly arrows represent and whether their representation is clear, use partial charges correctly and discriminately and check that the number of carbon atoms on the intermediate is correct.
notes.4bii: The equations described sometimes contained only pyruvic acid as a product or identified H rather than H O as a product.
notes.key_messages:
• Candidates who demonstrated a good knowledge of key definitions and applied well-rehearsed
arguments to appropriate situations scored more marks.
• Candidates who produced vague, imprecise definitions and used details of knowledge with less
accuracy and, on occasions, indiscriminately scored lower marks.
notes.general_comments:
Candidates are expected to balance all chemical equations.
Representation of equations to show specific reactions, for example ionisation energy of an element, should
contain all relevant details including state symbols.
